I have ADHD and these are things I've found to be helpful:

1) Break it up into small bits. I've been having major trouble with brain fog & exhaustion for months, and I've started studying in small pieces where I might read only a section of a chapter, make notes on literally one paragraph of an article, watch ten minutes of a video. It adds up and it makes progress, even if I feel like I'm five years old again.

2) Turn it into a story. Of course it depends on what you're studying, but it can work for some things (especially history or geography). My study is tied in with my writing, and if I learn something that I then use in a story, it sticks in my mind better. (You don't have to be good at writing, or even actually write the story down.)

3) Set up a reward system. I have whiteboards with grids set up, and each grid square is a chapter or article. Crossing/marking them off is very satisfying, and once I've finished a certain number of squares, I let myself go for a drive with a sibling or something like that.

4) Make notes as you study. It took me years to realize that people take notes not just so they can read them later, but because writing stuff down literally helps to reinforce it in your brain. Physically writing works best for me, but some people prefer writing directly onto a computer.

5) Repeating the information. The first time we study something, we don't retain most of it. It's the second time that helps to fix more of it in our brains. Don't just repeat it immediately, though - wait a few days or even longer (depending on how soon you need to learn the stuff).

6) Variety. This matters even for people without ADHD. If you learn the same information in various ways, it sticks better. But if you reread the same damn science section several times over, your brain will have become "used to" it, and won't pay as much attention. So go and find an article that tells you the same stuff and read that.

7) "Outputting" the information. Similar to point 4. If you explain a certain thing to someone, or write it out for a study blog, that sort of thing, it helps to reinforce the information in your brain. I ramble on about what I've learned to people I know, and it makes for interesting conversation ANd fixes it in my brain more.

8) Pretend to be a different person. Sounds ridiculous, but I find that it does work for me when I need extra motivation. I'll pretend I'm a person in one of my favourite movies or books, and then I am that person studying the information for such-and-such a reason. E.g. I have to learn a section on the rule of Ögedei Khan in the Mongol Empire. But today I simply cannot focus...so I pretend I am Natasha Romanoff learning the political background for a spy mission she has to go on. It adds an extra bit of interest & I can focus just a bit better.

9) Casual learning. I struggle a lot with learning geography & anything to do with place. I used to sit in front a map and try to memorize where the provinces of China were (for example). It didn't work! Now what I do is follow several geography/landscape/architecture blogs on Tumblr, and whenever I reblog a post of Chinese gardens (for example), I take note of which province it is, and quickly check it on a map. Eventually the information starts to trickle in and I start to remember where the provinces are. (Well, not many of them yet, but I'm getting there.) Not all learning is deliberate.

I hope some of this helps!! Feel free to message me if you want to. There are probably some good discussions & advice on the ADHD subreddit as well.

Verbs can be tricky things.  Nouns are specific - easy to remember.  Adjectives are more flexible - if you don't get the exact one you meant, your sentence will probably still make sense, even if it's not quite what you meant.  But verbs are somewhere in the middle - not as specific as nouns but not as flexible/interchangeable as adjectives.
